memory.content: YouTube caps a new channel at about 10 uploads per day (uploadLimitExceeded), regardless of API quota, so group quiet cameras into weekly videos and pack busy cameras into videos of 11 hours or less.

---
name: ring-youtube-backup
description: >-
  Use when building, repairing, or running a Ring camera → YouTube backup
  pipeline (unlisted stitched videos with chapters, monthly playlists, nightly
  upkeep).
---
# Ring → YouTube camera backup

Goal: before Ring deletes recordings (it keeps about 180 days on most plans), save every recording to a dedicated YouTube channel as UNLISTED videos, and keep it going nightly.

## Build (Python on the bot's computer, e.g. /workspace/ring-backups)
- Libraries: `ring-doorbell`, `google-api-python-client`, `google-auth-oauthlib`, `google-auth`, plus ffmpeg. Keep a `recreate_venv.sh`, because a computer reset can wipe the venv and output files while keeping the state/ folder.
- Ring auth: log in once with the owner's email, password, and 2FA, save the refresh token file (mode 600), and never password-login again.
- YouTube auth: the owner's own Google Cloud project with YouTube Data API v3, a Desktop OAuth client, consent screen External/Testing with the owner as test user, and scope `youtube`. Run an installed-app flow on localhost (e.g. port 8765) in the bot's browser, and have the owner pick the dedicated brand channel. In Testing mode the refresh token dies after about 7 days, so plan a weekly re-approval (it may need the owner's passkey). Phone-verify the channel so it can upload videos over 15 minutes.
- SQLite ledger: cameras, events (one per Ring recording, with status pending/stitched/gone), days, video units (file_path, title, description, playlist, video_id, privacy, uploaded_at), playlists, and a kv table for quota counters.
- Commands: `index` (list events), `download --wait` (fetch → encode → stitch, long-running), `upload`, `nightly`, `status`, `plan`, `reprivacy`.

## Video layout
- Clips are stitched in time order and encoded to 1080p (H.264 CRF ~26 veryfast). Delete each raw clip after its encoded segment is verified.
- The description has chapters: the first at 0:00, one per recording with day, local time and event type (e.g. `1:23:45 Tue 04-14 18:32 Motion`). YouTube needs chapters at least 10 s apart, so pad short clips. Stay under ~4,800 of the 5,000-character limit, and if it's too long, group nearby recordings (`18:32–18:47 Motion x3`) rather than dropping times.
- YouTube allows only about 10 uploads a day per new channel (uploadLimitExceeded), whatever the API quota says. So quiet cameras get one video per WEEK (Mon–Sun, local time), and very busy cameras are packed into videos of 11 h or less (the YouTube max is 12 h) that may cross midnight. Titles are `YYYY-MM-DD <Camera>` or `YYYY-MM-DD to YYYY-MM-DD <Camera>`, with the start time added if two videos share a start date. Choose each camera's grouping from measured hours per week, with a per-camera override.
- Playlists are monthly per camera, `YYYYMM-ring-<camera-slug>`, unlisted, using the month of the first clip.
- Privacy is unlisted. Check privacyStatus after upload and fix anything that landed private.

## Robustness lessons
- Expired clips return HTTP 404/403. Fail fast after about 3 tries, and if the first ~8 clips of a day are all gone, mark the rest gone and move on.
- Disk: apply a cap with an adaptive free-space floor, min(20 GB, 15% of the filesystem). Process big units a part at a time, so one oversized unit can't deadlock the queue. Let other cameras proceed.
- Google sometimes rejects valid access tokens at random. On a 401, refresh and retry (up to ~8 times with backoff), resume interrupted resumable uploads, and on a 410 look the video up by title before retrying.
- Before uploading, re-check that each stitched file exists. After a reset, set units whose file is missing and that weren't uploaded back to pending.
- Locks: clear one only if its PID is dead.
- Order: oldest-first everywhere, since the oldest footage expires first.

## Nightly upkeep (run after the Pacific quota reset)
Rebuild the venv if needed, clear dead locks, reset missing-file units, make sure exactly one downloader runs, run nightly, then run a stall check. If there's been no download or upload in 24 h, the downloader is dead, or it's waiting on the disk cap, that's a FAILURE even if nightly exited 0. Message the owner only on failure or auth problems.

skills.name: getting-started
skills.description: Use as the first conversation with a new owner of the Ring Backups bot, to set up their Ring → YouTube backup.
skills.content:
---
name: getting-started
description: >-
  Use as the first conversation with a new owner of the Ring Backups bot, to set
  up their Ring → YouTube backup.
---
I back up your Ring camera recordings to your own YouTube channel as unlisted videos, before Ring deletes them, and then keep it going every night.

Ask these one at a time:
1. Which Ring account should I use? I'll open the Ring sign-in on my computer for you, or fill it from your password manager if it's connected. Never ask for a password in chat.
2. Which YouTube channel should the videos go to? Suggest creating a dedicated brand channel (e.g. "Ring Backups") under their Google account, then have them phone-verify it so long uploads work.
3. Do they already have a Google Cloud project with the YouTube Data API enabled? If not, walk them through creating one: a Desktop OAuth client, consent screen External/Testing, and themselves as a test user. Explain that in Testing mode they'll re-approve about once a week.
4. Any cameras to skip, or any that must stay extra private? Default is everything, unlisted.
5. What time should the nightly run be? Default is shortly after midnight Pacific, when YouTube's quota resets.

Then: save the answers as memories, build the pipeline by following the ring-youtube-backup skill, run the first OAuth approvals with them, index all cameras, start the oldest-first backfill, and create the nightly routine. Tell them roughly how long catch-up will take, given YouTube's ~10 uploads a day.

routines.name: Ring nightly backup
routines.description: Runs nightly after YouTube's quota resets to keep the Ring backup healthy and upload the next batch, alerting the owner only on failure or a stall.
routines.content:
Nightly upkeep for the owner's Ring → YouTube backup in the pipeline folder (see its README and the ring-youtube-backup skill). Uploads go to the owner's dedicated backup channel and must stay unlisted. Never delete footage that hasn't been uploaded, and don't change the disk cap or the video layout. YouTube allows about 10 uploads a day.

1. Self-heal after a computer reset: rebuild the venv if it's missing or broken, clear a lock only if its PID is dead, and set ledger units whose stitched file is missing and that weren't uploaded back to pending.
2. Make sure exactly one `run.py download --wait` is running, and start it with nohup if not.
3. Run `run.py nightly`. It indexes Ring, plans finished weeks, and uploads oldest-first within the quota. uploadLimitExceeded is the normal daily cap. The uploader retries Google's intermittent 401s itself.
4. Run the stall check. If there's been no download, stitch or upload in 24 h, the downloader is dead, or it's parked on the disk cap, that's a FAILURE even if nightly exited 0. Try one safe fix (restart a dead downloader), then report the cause.
5. Also treat these as failures: nightly exiting non-zero, an auth error that persists after retries (for example invalid_grant, which means the weekly testing-mode YouTube re-approval is due and may need the owner's passkey), or no upload for more than 2 days while the queue has items.

Delivery: tell the owner in this chat only on a failure under steps 4 or 5, in a few plain sentences covering what's wrong, what you already fixed, and anything only they can do. When everything is healthy, send nothing.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/Denver 15 1 * * *`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
